articles.title: One UI 9 is finally rolling out to Galaxy S26 phones
articles.author: techkritiko@gmail.com (Jay Bonggolto) , Jay Bonggolto
articles.content:
What you need to know
- Samsung has started the stable One UI 9 update for the Galaxy S26 series, beginning in South Korea before expanding to other markets.
- One UI 9 brings features like My FanCam and more customizable Now Brief cards to the Galaxy S26 lineup.
- Samsung released seven beta builds over nearly five months, giving it time to fix bugs and refine the software.
Samsung has officially started the One UI 9 update rollout for the Galaxy S26 series, nearly five months after the company kicked off beta testing in May. The stable update for the Galaxy S26, S26 Plus, and S26 Ultra began rolling out in South Korea on September 16 and is now being released in other regions as well.
The test drive of the software wasn’t exactly a quick preview. Samsung released seven beta versions before moving to the finished release, allowing it to have several rounds of feedback and bug fixes to go through. The September security patch is, as expected, included with the stable release.
One UI 9 also includes some Galaxy AI features that first appeared on Samsung’s latest foldables. For example, one is the My FanCam feature, which can keep a chosen person in focus while automatically reframing video for different aspect ratios, while Now Brief gets customizable cards and expanded security and privacy information.
Samsung is also adding Now Nudge for more contextual suggestions and improvements to Interpreter, Document Scan, Voice Recorder summaries, and device care. Security Brief can find and surface warnings around malware, unknown apps, and unnecessary permissions, and on-device AI is able to identify potential privacy risks.
What’s interesting is how One UI 9 is moving away from a singular headline feature and is instead becoming more about tying Samsung’s AI, camera, and security tools into everyday tasks. That could make the update feel more substantial in daily use than the visual changes alone would suggest.
Samsung says One UI 9 will be available to more Galaxy phones and tablets, so international users should keep an eye on Settings > Software update > Download and install as the rollout expands to other markets.

Samsung has officially launched the stable One UI 9 update for the Galaxy S26 series, introducing new AI-driven camera features and enhanced security tools to global users.

### Key Points
- The stable One UI 9 rollout began in South Korea on September 16 for the Galaxy S26, S26 Plus, and S26 Ultra.
- Development included seven beta builds released over a five-month period to refine software stability and address user feedback.
- New features include My FanCam for automated video reframing and customizable Now Brief cards for improved information management.
- The update integrates the September security patch and adds advanced privacy tools like Security Brief to detect malware and unnecessary permissions.
- Enhanced AI capabilities now support Interpreter, Document Scan, and Voice Recorder summaries to streamline daily device tasks.

### Why it Matters
This update signals a strategic shift for Samsung, moving away from singular headline features toward integrating AI and security tools into core daily workflows. By prioritizing functional improvements over purely visual changes, the company aims to increase the long-term utility and security of its flagship mobile ecosystem.

articles.title: I switched from Google Password Manager to Bitwarden, and passwords weren't the reason
articles.author: Tashreef Shareef
articles.content:
Most of us started using Google Password Manager because it was built into Chrome. It was a no-brainer when a pop-up asked whether we wanted to save our username and password to the browser. The next time we visited the same website, Chrome would auto-fill the credentials, and that was it.
Beyond the small conveniences, though, Google's password manager is pretty basic. As my needs grew from storing passwords to wanting secure notes, file attachments, emergency access, and true cross-platform support, I switched to Bitwarden, which offers more transparency while being as secure as any paid password manager.
Secure notes and file attachments
More than just a password vault
Not everything you want to keep safe is a username and password. Software license keys, Wi-Fi passwords, account recovery codes, safe combinations, private notes: these are the kinds of things you'd otherwise scatter across sticky notes, random text files, or a notes app with no encryption. Google Password Manager has no place to put any of this. It stores login credentials, and that's about it.
You can use Bitwarden as a hub for all your sensitive data. Secure Notes let you store any free-form text you want behind encryption. I use them for API keys and backup codes that I'd rather not leave floating in my email inbox. Beyond notes, Bitwarden also supports Identity entries for auto-filling forms with your name, address, phone number, and email, and Card entries for storing credit card, debit card, or gift card details so you don't need the physical card at checkout.
Premium subscribers ($10 per year) can also attach files to any vault item, which is useful for scanned documents or PDFs you want encrypted alongside the credentials they belong to.
Emergency access
A plan for when you can't log in yourself
This is one of those features you hope you'll never need, but you'll be glad it exists if you do. Bitwarden's Emergency Access lets you designate a trusted contact who can request access to your vault if you're incapacitated or unreachable.
For this to work, your contact needs a Bitwarden account (the free tier works fine), and you invite them through the app. The system uses public-key encryption in a zero-knowledge setup, meaning Bitwarden never sees your master password. If an emergency arises, the contact requests access, and you get notified so you can approve or deny it. If you don't respond, it auto-approves after a wait time you've set in advance. Depending on the access level you choose, they get either read-only view access or full takeover rights to set a new master password.
Emergency Access is a premium feature, but at $10 per year, it's significantly cheaper than similar offerings from competitors like 1Password or Dashlane. Google Password Manager doesn't offer anything like this at all.
True cross-platform support
Use any browser, any device, any OS
Google Password Manager works well if you live entirely inside Chrome and Google's ecosystem. However, there's no standalone app for managing your vault on desktop or even on Android. You need Chrome open to access anything.
Bitwarden offers true cross-platform support. It has native apps for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android. For browsers, it covers all the Chromium-based ones like Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Brave, plus non-Chromium options like Safari, Firefox, DuckDuckGo, and even Tor. On top of that, there's a web vault you can access from any browser and a command-line tool for more technical setups.
Also, it's consistent across platforms. Bitwarden looks and behaves the same whether I'm on my laptop, phone, or switching between browsers. There's no learning curve when I move between devices, so it's easy to find what I am looking for irrespective of where I am using the password manager.
Organized vaults and sharing
Keep it tidy, share it safely
The longer you use a password manager, the more cluttered it gets. Google Password Manager gives you a flat list of saved logins and not much else. Bitwarden offers a bit more structure through Collections, which let you group credentials and share different sets with different people.
For example, you could create one collection of streaming passwords your partner has full access to, and a separate collection of accounts your child can only view. Free and Premium accounts get two collections, while the Families plan offers unlimited ones. Access can also be scoped by role, with Admin, Manager, and User levels available for more structured sharing.
For one-off sharing, Bitwarden Send creates an encrypted link you can send to anyone, even if they're not a Bitwarden user. You can set an expiration date, a maximum number of accesses, and a password. Free users can share text, while Premium subscribers can also share files. It's a much cleaner way to share sensitive data than texting a password in plain text, which is what most people end up doing.
Passkey support
Ready for the passwordless future
Passkeys are quickly becoming a better alternative to passwords across major services like Google, Apple, and Microsoft. Google Password Manager does support passkeys, but it stores them within its own ecosystem, and until recently, moving them elsewhere was not an option. As of June 2026, Google has started rolling out passkey import and export using the FIDO Alliance's Credential Exchange standard, but the rollout is still limited and depends on third-party apps supporting it too.
Bitwarden was one of the first password managers to support both creating and managing passkeys. You can set it as your default passkey provider on Android (14 and above) or Windows, and it handles passkey creation and authentication across its browser extensions, mobile apps, and desktop clients. So your passkeys aren't locked to one platform or one device.
The bigger picture here is, of course, portability. One of the main criticisms of passkeys has been that they're device-bound, making it hard to move passkeys between password managers without starting from scratch. Bitwarden's early adoption of the Credential Exchange standard means you can move your passkeys in and out without being trapped. For someone like me who is adopting passkeys wherever possible, this is a must-have in a password manager
Stop storing passwords in your browser
Migrating from Google Password Manager to Bitwarden took me about ten minutes. You export your saved passwords from Chrome's settings as a CSV file, import it into Bitwarden, and you're done. The browser extension takes over auto-fill duties right away, and the mobile app handles the rest.
While some features do need a subscription, the free plan covers the basics well enough and doesn't keep bugging you to upgrade every few minutes. If you're still relying on your browser's built-in password manager, it might be worth considering a dedicated one. You'll be surprised how much more they can do beyond just saving passwords
articles.summary:
Bitwarden offers a more robust, cross-platform alternative to Google Password Manager by providing advanced features like secure notes, emergency access, and flexible credential sharing for all users.

### Key Points
- Bitwarden supports secure notes, file attachments, and identity storage, whereas Google Password Manager is limited to basic login credentials.
- The platform provides native applications for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android, ensuring consistent access across all browsers and devices.
- Premium subscriptions cost $10 per year, offering features like emergency access and file storage that are unavailable in Google’s built-in tool.
- Bitwarden enables organized credential sharing through collections and secure, encrypted links via the Bitwarden Send feature.
- The service supports passkey management and adheres to the FIDO Alliance's Credential Exchange standard to prevent platform lock-in.

### Why it Matters
Transitioning to a dedicated password manager improves digital security by centralizing sensitive data and enabling cross-platform portability that browser-based tools lack. This shift allows users to maintain better control over their credentials and passkeys while ensuring access remains available during emergencies.

articles.title: Blizzard’s Got A Serious Scalping Problem On Its Hands
articles.author: Rebekah Valentine
articles.content:
On day 0 of BlizzCon 2026—like, the Friday before the event when you could pick up your badge but there was no con going on yet—the line for the Blizzard merch store was several hours long. It snaked all over the hall. I have friends who stood in it for two, three hours, just for the opportunity to spend money. I saw that line at about 3pm, said “Nope” out loud to myself, and left.
Then, one of my friends who was in the line sent me a photo of a con-goer who had obtained this item:
Oh! That’s Pepe! The little orange bird friend from World of Warcraft whom I love! I have a little Pepe of my own at home, yes. But my Pepe is not wearing a cozy little fur cloak and holding a tiny cup of cocoa and marshmallows like this one is. I’m rarely one to be swayed by merchandise, but I asked my friend to grab me one if he saw one when he got to the front of the line. Obviously, by the time he did, they were sold out.
I initially brushed this off. Pepe is very popular, obviously many people would want to purchase one, and I didn’t need more plushes lying around. But as BlizzCon went on, it became increasingly apparent that BlizzCon, and Blizzard more broadly, is developing a serious scalper problem. And worse, Blizzard itself isn’t doing all that much to curb it.
Part of the problem is the exclusivity of many items you could obtain from BlizzCon. As I said, Pepe himself selling out isn’t shocking. He’s very well-loved. It’s irritating to see several of him listed as sold on eBay for as much as $155 when, at the show, he only cost around $30, but I’ll get over that. But lots of other, far more egregious resales are going on, empowered by artificial scarcity. For instance, BlizzCon includes an event called the Darkmoon Faire. The Darkmoon Faire is popular and has a limited capacity, so you have to stand in a long line to get into it. Once inside, the Faire is full of activities, freebies, a bustling hub of pin trading and collecting, and more things to buy. For instance, there’s a duck pond where you first have to purchase a ticket, then wait in line to use it, then use a fishing rod to catch a random duck from a pond, then—if you happened to get a duck with a star on it—you get a code for an exclusive World of Warcraft in-game pet.
So let me recap that again: you have to buy a BlizzCon pass, stand in the long line to get into BlizzCon, then stand in another really long line for the Darkmoon Faire, then make a purchase, then stand in another really long line, all for a random chance at getting a robotic duck in World of Warcraft that you can’t get anywhere else. Oh, yeah, and codes for these ducks are all over eBay, with actual sales as high as $600 just for this pet. You’ve got to be kidding me!
Let’s think about Pepe again real quick: also in the Darkmoon Faire, there’s a $30 plushie blind box you can stand in line to buy that includes one of eight different plush toys, including Pepe. Blind boxes are nothing new, but purchasers also had a random chance to receive a code with their box for another pet: a flying axolotl. These, too, are selling on eBay for as much as $500 a pop! What are we doing here? Why is this a gacha game?
This is, as far as we know, the only way there is or ever will be to get any of these pets. And look, World of Warcraft pets have been somewhat of a meme for years. People who love them love them, but a lot of players just ignore them, as they don’t really have much function outside of aesthetics and a silly, Pokémon-like battle system that’s fully optional to ever engage with. But it still sucks that for people who do care about such things, these pets are locked behind not just an event ticket purchase, but also multiple lines, another purchase, and random chance. The natural result of this is that people with cash to burn are absolutely going to slurp up as many as they can, take them home, and resell them for exorbitant amounts of money. It doesn’t have to be this way!
And this isn’t just limited to BlizzCon merchandise. World of Warcraft: Forever, which was revealed at the show, comes in (among other, cheaper variants) a shiny Collector’s Edition costing $150. It comes with the game bundle in question as well as a bunch of shiny goodies like a big ol’ statuette, pins, art prints, and an admittedly nice-looking mousepad. This edition of the game is purchasable online, but has sold out, been restocked, and sold out again multiple times in the three days since it was announced. Tons of players are complaining online that they can’t purchase a single one for themselves even if they open the store right as they receive the restock alert, claiming it has sold out within seconds each time.
Meanwhile, we’ve got this crap going on:
Ugh! Why! As one person points out on Reddit, these editions are not restricted to individuals with existing Battle.net accounts. And while it says only three can be purchased per household, you can just use different emails to get around that restriction and get as many as you want if you’ve got the tech to snap them up fast:
I have some sympathy for Blizzard here; online scalpers are getting increasingly clever at finding ways around protections, and there are so many of them anymore that you’re always going to have at least a few causing issues, no matter what you do. But it’s hard not to see Blizzard as at least a little complicit, even if inadvertently, in both of these situations. It designed this absurd gacha system of pet codes at BlizzCon, and it had fairly lax restrictions on Collector’s Edition purchases. We’ll have to see what restocks on the Collector’s Edition look like in the coming days, as that may alleviate some of the tension, though in that case I feel bad for the poor saps who already dumped hundreds of dollars more than the retail price on an item they could have just bought anyway.
God, the scalper economy sucks. If it’s not Blizzard, it’s Pokémon, or concert tickets, or something else. Shame to everyone contributing to this crap. Both Pepe and myself think it’s embarrassing.
articles.summary:
BlizzCon 2026 attendees are facing significant frustration as limited-edition merchandise and exclusive in-game digital rewards are being rapidly purchased by scalpers for resale at exorbitant prices online.

### Key Points
- Exclusive World of Warcraft in-game pet codes from the Darkmoon Faire are appearing on eBay for as much as $600.
- Popular merchandise, such as a $30 Pepe plushie, is being resold for over $150 after selling out at the event.
- The $150 World of Warcraft: Forever Collector’s Edition has repeatedly sold out online within seconds due to automated purchasing tactics.
- Critics argue that Blizzard’s use of "gacha-style" random chance mechanics for physical and digital items encourages aggressive scalping behavior.
- Current purchase restrictions, such as household limits, are easily bypassed by scalpers using multiple email addresses and automated software.

### Why it Matters
The prevalence of scalping at major gaming events creates significant barriers for dedicated fans who are priced out of collecting exclusive items. This trend highlights a growing tension between companies using artificial scarcity to drive engagement and the resulting negative impact on consumer trust and community accessibility.

articles.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
articles.author: Louise Matsakis
articles.content:
For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous, tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down.
“Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “We Must Pace the Frontier.”
China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal.
“The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.”
Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies.
“His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.”
Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”)
The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained.
When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.”
The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power.
“Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.”
In a recent essay, China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs.
“Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.”
That skepticism is also shared by many people who work in China’s AI industry, which has broadly focused on releasing lower-cost, open-weight models. In a widely shared essay published on Sunday, a researcher at DeepSeek said he believes AI could move human society to one of two extremes. In the first, powerful AI is broadly available and raises living standards. In the second, a handful of tech companies control the most advanced systems and the resources that come with them, making it even harder for everyone else to catch up.
“That is why I still believe the most advanced intelligence should be made available to everyone in an open and inexpensive way,” the DeepSeek engineer wrote. “I do not trust Anthropic or OpenAI to do that. And I especially do not want Anthropic to control the most advanced artificial intelligence or AGI.”
None of this means that US-China cooperation on AI safety is doomed. Preliminary negotiations between the two countries are reportedly already underway ahead of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington later this month to meet with US President Donald Trump.
There are plenty of reasons to be hopeful that these discussions will result in some progress, even though it may be incremental. Both governments have expressed worries about some of the same things, including cybersecurity threats, the misuse of powerful models, and the possibility that increasingly capable AI systems could behave in unexpected ways.
“There are people who genuinely care about AI safety on both sides, and there’s a possibility they could engage in good-faith discussion in narrowly scoped issues,” says Nie. What might move the needle most, she says, is designing a credible way for each country to verify that the other is abiding by its commitments.
Still, others worry that rhetoric from Amodei and other US tech leaders about weakening China could erode the fragile trust that diplomatic talks depend on. Kristy Loke, a research fellow at the AI safety nonprofit MATS Research, says that Amodei’s missive may ultimately backfire. “Dario is undermining one of the few available levers for reducing the very risks he professes to take seriously,” she says.
articles.summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is calling for US-China cooperation on AI safety, though his proposal to maintain American technological dominance has faced significant skepticism from Chinese officials.

### Key Points
- Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a blog post urging the US and China to collaborate on slowing the development of dangerous frontier AI models.
- Amodei’s strategy includes maintaining a US lead by restricting Chinese access to advanced chips and preventing unauthorized model distillation.
- China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected the proposal, labeling it as "fearmongering" and a form of "vicious competition" rather than genuine cooperation.
- Chinese leadership prioritizes AI risks related to social stability and Communist Party control over the existential "doomsday" scenarios often cited by Silicon Valley.
- Researchers at Chinese firms like DeepSeek argue that US tech companies are using safety narratives to stifle competition and consolidate market power.
- Preliminary diplomatic negotiations regarding AI safety are reportedly underway ahead of a planned meeting between President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.

### Why it Matters
The tension between US tech leaders and Beijing highlights the difficulty of establishing global AI governance when national security and economic competition remain primary drivers. If these diplomatic efforts fail, the lack of a unified safety framework could increase the risk of uncontrolled AI development and geopolitical instability.

articles.title: SK Hynix is in talks with Intel to make memory chips in the US, Reuters reports
articles.author: Ana-Maria Stanciuc
articles.content:
According to an exclusive Reuters report, based on information from three individuals involved in the talks, SK Hynix is negotiating a deal that would mark the first time the South Korean company manufactures memory chips in the United States.
One possibility is for the company to lease part of Intel’s chip-making site in Ohio, and another is to form a joint venture with Intel and major cloud providers to secure a steady supply of memory.
A source stated that no decisions had been reached, and SK Hynix told Reuters that it was looking at “a number of measures, including the establishment of further production bases”, but added that no agreement had been reached. Intel refused to comment on what it called speculation, although it said it is still investing in preparing its site in Ohio.
In July, Korea JoongAng Daily stated that SK Hynix was negotiating to buy the entire campus with a view to beginning front-end memory production within five years. According to Reuters, the arrangement would be either a lease or a joint venture, and in either case, the companies have not confirmed it.
SK Hynix is also under pressure, according to a January Bloomberg report. US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has stated that South Korean and Taiwanese chipmakers could face tariffs of up to 100% if they do not agree to establish operations in America.
The company holds a leading position in the high-bandwidth memory market, which involves stacked chips placed alongside AI processors, and demand from data centers has led to a memory shortage.
The current US commitment refers only to the later stage of the process. SK Hynix is constructing a $4bn packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana, at which HBM will be packaged rather than manufactured.
According to Reuters, producing the memory itself in the United States would be more expensive, as labor, construction, and the supplier base all add to the cost compared with production at home.
Although the South Korean Ministry of Trade stated that the final decision lies with the company, it added that a deal involving a ‘national core technology’ would be examined under the country’s Industrial Technology Protection Act.
The investors responded promptly; according to Stocktwits, Intel increased by about 5% and the US-listed shares of SK Hynix by about 3% in overnight trading following the report. SK Hynix had added those US shares in July when it went public on the Nasdaq.

articles.summary:
SK Hynix is currently negotiating a potential deal to manufacture memory chips in the United States, possibly by leasing space at Intel’s semiconductor production site in Ohio.

### Key Points
- SK Hynix is considering a joint venture or lease agreement with Intel to establish its first domestic memory chip production facility in the United States.
- The company is currently building a $4 billion advanced packaging plant in West Lafayette, Indiana, which does not include front-end chip manufacturing.
- US Commerce officials have suggested that foreign chipmakers could face significant tariffs if they do not expand their manufacturing operations within the country.
- SK Hynix holds a dominant market position in high-bandwidth memory, a critical component currently experiencing supply shortages due to high demand from AI data centers.
- Any final agreement involving this technology must be reviewed by the South Korean government under the Industrial Technology Protection Act.

### Why it Matters
Establishing domestic memory production would help the United States secure its semiconductor supply chain and reduce reliance on overseas manufacturing for critical AI hardware. This move could significantly lower geopolitical risks for major cloud providers while increasing operational costs for SK Hynix due to higher American labor and construction expenses.

articles.title: Apple’s Health App Hits Developer Beta. I Got the Inside Scoop From Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness
articles.author: Anna Gragert
articles.content:
Last week at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness, announced the redesigned Health app and its fresh features. Between the new Insights tab with Apple Intelligence-powered suggestions, a Longevity tab that shows your Health Age, a readiness score, movement assessments, a blood panel and curated doctor videos, my head was swimming with questions. The following day, I sat down for a video chat with Desai for deeper insight into Apple’s reimagined health platform.
Now, on Wednesday, the new Health app debuted in the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. Some announced features will be available in later betas, including personalized summaries under the Insights tab, personalized recommendations and the ability to order a blood panel from Quest Diagnostics.
“Features will roll out progressively,” Apple said in an email. “Feedback during the beta period will help us continue refining it ahead of the public release in late 2026.”
Here’s everything you can expect to uncover in the Health app and the features you shouldn’t sleep on.
From data spreadsheet to intelligent experience
Launched in 2014, the Health app was initially intended to be like a spreadsheet, with data flowing in, Desai explained. However, the team realized they wanted more from the app, so it evolved over the past 12 years into what Desai now calls “an experience.”
Those at the helm of the Health app’s 2026 makeover considered how to leverage Apple’s machine learning and AI to help people live healthier, while also personalizing the app’s recommendations and turning it into an intelligent hub, not unlike the iPhone itself. For instance, as you open the app and move through your day, different screens appear to reflect your health status.
Movement assessments have also been added to provide an even more complete picture of a user’s health and track progress or decline. Desai described them as a “mini physical” you can complete at home.
All assessments under the app’s Longevity tab are science-based and contribute to a rainbow-petal visual that illuminates your state of health. Some assessments rely on vision-based AI models that integrate the phone’s camera, marking the first time Apple has used the camera for health.
The current iteration of the Health app is just the beginning and was designed to set in motion the next era of the team’s work in health and fitness, as Desai said those working on the app still feel they have more to do.
Health Age: Biological vs. birthday
One standout feature from Apple’s event was the Health app’s Longevity tab, which will include a feature called Health Age that uses health metrics such as your VO2 max (the maximum amount of oxygen your body consumes during exercise), resting heart rate, sleep and heart rate variability, along with lab data such as LDL cholesterol and A1c for your average blood sugar level, to provide your biological age, which represents how your body is aging on a cellular level when compared to your actual age.
Apple’s own Heart and Movement Study, which it applies across all its health products, informs both Health Age and Readiness, which uses your activity data, daytime and overnight vitals and sleep data to tell you about your capacity for the day ahead.
The five-year Heart and Movement Study was conducted in collaboration with the American Heart Association and Brigham and Women’s Hospital to explore the connection between heart health and physical activity. Apple used that data to create the normative ranges for the insights it provides in the app.
While Desai acknowledged the Health Age assessment is more of a “fun way to look at your health habits” and that no one can tell you your actual biological age, it’s another way to provide insight and suggest healthy habits users can integrate into their lives.
Apple’s secret sauce
Apple isn’t the first company to offer features such as a readiness score or biological age, but Desai said that it stands out from competitors because of its unique perspectives, experiences and the science behind its work.
“When we first started our work in health, when we announced our irregular heart rhythm notifications and ECG, those were clinically validated scientific features,” she said. Desai likened those early days to building a muscle that lets the team create impactful products the medical community will appreciate, and users can easily understand.
That muscle Apple first built has been exercised with all the Health app’s new features, as Desai said that everything is rooted in science. On her team, for instance, physical therapists graded each movement in the app’s mobility assessments to ensure that when a movement is picked up and a result is given, it’s graded the way an actual physical therapist would grade it.
Uniting science and expertise, Desai said that’s what Apple brings to the table, and its Health app experience.
The new Health app’s ‘sleeper hit’
Much of the discourse following Apple’s event has been about the new readiness score and Health Age. I was curious what Desai felt was the “sleeper hit” feature that didn’t get as much attention.
“It’s actually the assessments,” Desai said. “You’re going to be able to, on a regular basis, do a push-up test and a core test and see if you’re improving. Then we give you insights and things that you can do to improve, and then you can test again. It’s almost like having a physical therapist or a trainer.”
The VO2 max test, in particular, marks the first time Apple’s doing an on-demand, in-the-moment VO2 max test.
You can then take all your assessment results, and the Health app will put them into a report you can share with your doctor.
Homing in on your body’s big players
Based on its new assessments, the Longevity tab’s visualization has seven tabs: heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition. But how did Apple narrow it down to those seven?
“We picked areas where we felt like we had the appropriate data to comment on,” Desai explained. “For example, we do a cardiovascular risk score through some of the questions. It’s based on traditional risk scores and cardiovascular risk scores that are done.”
The team prioritized information they believe people will use and assessments they’ll complete, while ensuring the chosen health areas feel holistic and will help people concerned about long-term quality of life.
“There’s still more that we think we can do, but this is where we’re starting,” Desai stated. In other words, Longevity’s rainbow visual could gain more colors in the future.
Keeping privacy at Apple’s core
When it comes to its Health app, Desai said privacy is where they start and end.
“Candidly, we may not always be the first to market, but when we release something, we can stand behind it from a privacy standpoint,” Desai stated. “All the features you saw [announced] are no different. … It’s part of the conversation every day, and up till the day that the products are launched.”
Apple will hold off on releasing a product if it hasn’t met its privacy bar. The team behind the Health app also uses a checks-and-balances system, having other teams review their work to ensure they are nailing their privacy approach.
“In this world where more things happen in the cloud, we want to make sure that’s all encrypted and private, which is why we have Private Cloud Compute,” said Desai. Private Cloud Compute is Apple’s cloud intelligence system designed for private AI processing.
The team’s approach is end-to-end because privacy matters for all your data, not just health data.
Apple Intelligence has suggestions
The Health app’s new Insights tab uses Apple Intelligence to analyze your health metrics and provide a timely summary that updates throughout the day.
“We also make suggestions,” said Desai. “For example, if you have an injury or you’re trying to work on your mobility, we’ll give you suggestions on the types of exercises you might be doing.”
It’s another example of how the app is evolving from a database to something that more closely resembles a personalized health advisor.
The daily insights are meant to be bite-size pieces of information that are one small thing you can do for your health each day. Some days these insights may be interesting; other days, you might be given information you already know.
Health on a cellular level, explained
For $119, the new Health app will let you purchase a blood panel with over 50 biomarkers through Quest Diagnostics. You can also get your blood pressure, height, weight and waist and hip circumferences measured. All this helps provide a more complete picture of metabolic health.
The revamped app will include videos from doctors that help people better understand what they see in the app.
“When you get your assessment results, you’ll actually see your own data in the videos where they’re explained by clinicians,” said Desai. “We have a physician, a physical therapist, a sleep expert, a mental health expert. The reason we did that is, for certain things, gamification works, but for certain things, you just want to know the information in an easy-to-understand way from an authoritative resource.”
While an expert explains the subject at hand, your health data, whether from your labs or your Apple Watch, will be overlaid on the video so you can see it as you learn more.
Ultimately, Desai doesn’t see the future of the Health app as one size fits all. Depending on the feature, the team always chooses what makes health as accessible and understandable as possible. In a world with an abundance of health data, perhaps that’s what matters most: ensuring people understand the numbers they see on their devices, and knowing what to do with them once the screen goes black.

### Key Points
- The new Longevity tab features a "Health Age" metric, calculating biological age using VO2 max, heart rate variability, sleep data, and lab results.
- Apple introduced vision-based AI movement assessments, allowing users to perform physical therapy-style tests at home using their iPhone camera.
- A new Insights tab leverages Apple Intelligence to provide personalized, daily health summaries and actionable exercise recommendations.

- All health data processing is secured through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute to ensure end-to-end encryption and user privacy.

### Why it Matters
This update signals Apple’s strategic shift from a passive data repository to an active, intelligent health management hub that competes with specialized wellness platforms. By integrating clinical-grade assessments and AI-driven guidance, Apple aims to make complex medical data more accessible and actionable for the average consumer.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang clashed at Dreamforce over whether the artificial intelligence industry should slow development to implement stricter safety and regulatory standards.

### Key Points
- Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed embedding third-party evaluators and coordinating international safety standards to manage the rapid pace of AI development.
- Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argued against government regulation, suggesting companies should independently ensure product safety before release rather than slowing innovation.
